extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, translators, and students of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reading, defending, and judging epic poetry (especially Homer): how to resolve apparent errors, justify marvelous or archaic expressions, and assess poetic language and design. Emphasises textual, historical, and genre-aware methods of interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admirable use of metaphor and personification in the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor (e.g., attributing voice to inanimate or mute things) is of wonderful use in the sublime and should be admired rather than censured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Voice of thy Thunder' and 'The Voice of thy Brother's Blood cryeth to me from the Ground.' Such personifications heighten the sublime and are appropriate in epic description (e.g., Nabum's description of the destruction of Nineveh). Do not condemn these for literal impossibility; they function as elevated metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent errors by altering accent or accentuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some passages that appear false or obscene can be justified by an alternate placement of the accent (intonation) in the original language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hippias' defense of Homer where a line read as a lie (Jupiter making a false promise) is rescued by shifting the accent so the imperative sense (Give him) is intended. Translators and critics should check accentual possibilities before condemning a passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve bad or contradictory readings via punctuation/pointing
rubrics_metrics.description: False punctuation (points) can spoil sense and produce accusations of contradiction; re‑pointing the text often restores coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Empedocles' verses appeared self-contradictory until the point was transposed. Quintilian discussed this vice. Translators should consider alternate punctuation as a remedy for apparent contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine all possible meanings of polysemous words
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word seems to mean something contrary to the poet's intention, one must inspect every different signification the word can have in that passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Critics read 'stopt' as 'remained fixed' and ridiculed Homer, but 'stopt' could mean 'could go no further' (i.e., was repelled). Always survey alternate lexical senses before complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take words in a contrary or atypical sense when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the shortest way to explain a passage is to take a word in the opposite of its ordinary sense, especially in Greek where words often have contrary meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The unequal exchange of arms is best read as a noble act (elevated courage) rather than foolish—Porphyry and commentators give opposite-sense readings. Translators should be open to such inversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the probable-impossible over the merely possible-but-unbelievable in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and epic-like poetry should favour the 'probable impossible' (marvelous but plausible within the genre) rather than literal possibilities lacking verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Poetry mixes history and fable; the admirable and marvelous are proper. Example: Vulcan's self-moving chariots on Achilles' shield—though extraordinary, they are believable as the work of a god and serve the poem's grandeur. Critics who demand only mundane possibility misunderstand epic genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify unusual expressions by contemporary custom and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions that seem improper (e.g., wine mixed with water called 'wine'; princes performing humble tasks) can be justified by usage and historical custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage is 'the tyrant of languages'—do not condemn Homer for terms that were ordinary in his culture. Biblical parallels often show similar language; customs (e.g., princes slaying victims themselves) explain depictions that later audiences find odd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect historical and cultural context (manners) when evaluating style
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess descriptions and epithets against the customs and values of the poet's age rather than against modern sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Calling Ajax an ass or Ulysses 'fat' had different connotations historically; asses were ridden by kings; 'fat' related to sacrificial wealth. Critics must study ancient manners (e.g., Thessaly's retained simplicity) before passing judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anachronistic or prejudiced criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics who begin with modern presuppositions (e.g., geography was well known or unknown) condemn poets unfairly; one should not read prejudices into ancient texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Accusations that Homer was ignorant of astronomy or geography often stem from critics' preconceptions. Examine the poet within his own intellectual milieu and consult ancient authorities (Strabo, others) rather than projecting later standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intentional ambiguity to reconcile problematic quantitative phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that seem numerically or logically odd may be reconciled by reading ambiguous qualifiers in a different sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'More than two thirds of the night are past, and one alone remains'—read 'more than' to mean 'the greater part' (i.e., two thirds) rather than a strict arithmetic clause. Consult commentators for plausible readings before rejecting a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult textual traditions and authoritative commentators before judging
rubrics_metrics.description: Before condemning a line or reading, survey the manuscript tradition, commentators, local traditions, and ancient authorities for alternative explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Strabo's defense of Homer on the Bear constellation; Eustathius and the Pythagorean Damo's commentary on Achilles' shield; traditional accounts about Icarius. Scholars should consult these sources as they may decisively answer criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the poet's intention and design before criticizing subject or manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what the poet aimed to represent (e.g., the universe on Achilles' shield) and judge subject and manner relative to that intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Critics who call the shield's subject trivial ignore that Homer intends to depict the universe and human occupations in order and probability. Recognize the scope and design of an image prior to fault-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain marvelous elements by genre logic (divine or original agency) rather than literal impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Marvels in epic (animated figures, moving devices) should be explained by the poem's logic—gods, original models, or artistic hyperbole—rather than condemned for mechanical impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ancient tales of self-moving statues and Platonic reports that Dedalus' statues walked provide precedent; Vulcan's animated wheels are appropriate to divine craftsmanship. Also point out technological analogues (mechanical automata) to reduce perceived impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics must be well-informed and cautious; avoid hasty condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: One should only pass judgment after acquiring requisite knowledge of language, customs, textual variants, and genre; otherwise praise or blame will be unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against 'blind critics' who condemn what is not agreeable to their taste. Training, learning, and humility are prerequisites for fair criticism; otherwise one risks absurdities and unjust censure.
